title: Choosing & adapting a life cycle
blurb: Explain how an organisation's context and culture, and a project's own needs, shape the choice of life cycle and the adaptations it may need.
question: A medical-devices company wants a new app for clinicians. The clinicians' needs are unclear and will emerge as they try it, but the regulator requires documented approval before anything is released, and the company has always run projects with formal sign-offs. Which life cycle should the project manager propose, and how might it need adapting?

teach.h: There is no single best life cycle
teach.body: The right life cycle is the one that fits two things: the context and culture of the organisation, and the needs of this particular project. Choosing well, and then adapting (tailoring) the chosen model, gives the project the right balance of control and flexibility. In plain English: look at the organisation you're in and the job in front of you, pick the model that suits both, then adjust it so it works in practice.

teach.h: Which way does each factor point?
head: Factor
Points to linear
Points to iterative
rows: Benefits at the end are fine
teach.caption: Real projects rarely point one way on every factor, which is why adaptation and hybrid approaches exist.

teach.h: Culture matters as much as the work
teach.body: An organisation's governance approach shapes the project's governance. A business with a strong command-and-control culture, heavy approval chains and no agile experience may struggle with pure iterative working even when requirements are uncertain: decisions stall, product owners aren't empowered, and time boxes slip. The reverse also applies: a fast-moving digital firm may find a heavily gated linear model frustrating. Either adapt the life cycle to the culture, or build capability (training, coaching, a pilot) before relying on it.

teach.h: A rule of thumb (not an APM rule)
teach.caption: Uncertain needs in a control-minded organisation is the tricky quadrant: adapt the model rather than force a pure one.

teach.h: Typical ways to adapt a life cycle
items: Add decision gates or formal approvals to an iterative model, for example before each release to a regulated client.
Add prototyping or user trials inside a linear Definition phase to test uncertain requirements early.
Split linear Deployment into releases or tranches so some benefits arrive sooner.
Combine or lighten phases and gates on a small, low-risk project.
Add Adoption and Benefits realisation (the extended life cycle) where benefits arrive after handover.
Mix approaches by workstream (a hybrid life cycle) where certainty differs across the work.

teach.h: A typical way to choose and adapt

steps.label:
Agree and
record
steps.sub: Sponsor approves; documented in the PMP

steps.label: Review
steps.sub: Revisit at gates and reviews if things change

teach.body: Project needs: clinicians can't yet say what they want, so iterative suits the build. Organisational context: a regulator needs documented approval before release, and Medisure is used to formal sign-offs. So the project manager proposes an iterative life cycle adapted with a formal gate after Foundations (approving the business case and plan) and a regulatory approval gate before each release goes live. The sponsor approves the approach, and it is recorded in the project management plan.

teach.text: The weak answer is 'choose the method the project manager or team prefers' or 'software is always iterative, construction is always linear'. The choice comes from the FACTORS: the organisation's context and culture plus the project's needs. And adapting a life cycle never means dropping governance; it means making the governance fit the way the work is done.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Name the organisational factors in the scenario (regulation, contracts, culture, skills, stakeholder availability).
Name the project factors (requirement certainty, complexity, risk, urgency, size).
Say which life cycle they point to, and why.
Describe at least one specific adaptation (for example, adding gates to iterative for a regulator).
Note that the choice is agreed with the sponsor, recorded in the PMP and revisited if circumstances change.
Two sets of influences: organisational context and culture, and the needs of the project.
Context: governance, regulation, contracts, maturity, existing methods, skills, availability, appetite for change.
Project needs: requirement certainty, complexity, risk, urgency, need for early benefits, size.
The chosen model is usually tailored, for example gates added to iterative for a regulated client.
Record the approach in the PMP and revisit it at gates and reviews.

summary: You can now explain how an organisation's context and culture and a project's own needs drive the choice of life cycle. You can also describe practical adaptations, such as adding gates to an iterative model, and justify them in a written answer.

A.q: Which pair of influences should drive the choice of a project's life cycle?
options: Industry sector and the PM's experience
The last project's method and its budget
A.why: The choice rests on the organisation's context and culture together with the needs of the specific project.

whyNot.0: Sector and one person's experience are not enough; the same sector can need different approaches.
whyNot.2: Supplier preference and price are only part of the organisational context.
whyNot.3: Copying the last project ignores this project's own needs.

A.q: An organisation's culture is strongly hierarchical, and every decision needs a senior manager's sign-off. How might this affect an iterative approach?
options: Slow decisions may stall time boxes
It will make the scope easier to fix
It removes the need for a product owner
It guarantees early delivery of value
A.why: Iterative working relies on quick decisions by an empowered product owner. Long approval chains can stall each time box.

whyNot.1: Iterative scope flexes by design; hierarchy doesn't fix it.
whyNot.2: Iterative working still needs a product owner, ideally an empowered one.
whyNot.3: Slow decisions make early value harder, not guaranteed.

A.q: A regulated client insists on formal approval before anything goes live, but the requirements are uncertain. Which adaptation is most appropriate?
options: Remove the reviews to speed delivery
Fix the full scope before Feasibility
Add approval gates to iterative work
A.why: Iterative working handles the uncertain requirements, and added gates meet the client's need for formal approval before release.

whyNot.0: Removing reviews would breach the client's approval requirement.
whyNot.1: Fixing full scope up front ignores the uncertainty in the requirements.
whyNot.3: Skipping Foundations removes the agreed priorities and plan the regulator would expect.

B.q: A small, low-risk internal project with clear requirements is being planned with the organisation's full linear model, including five formal gates. Which adaptation is most appropriate?
options: Add more gates for extra control
B.why: Project size and risk are project needs. A small, low-risk project doesn't need the full weight of governance, so phases and gates can be combined or lightened.

whyNot.0: More gates add cost and delay with little benefit on a small, low-risk project.
whyNot.1: Parallel workstreams are a hybrid pattern for mixed certainty; requirements here are clear.
whyNot.2: Adoption comes after Transition, never before Concept.

B.q: Which is NOT an organisational context factor when choosing a life cycle?
B.why: Requirement certainty is a need of the PROJECT, not a feature of the organisation's context.

whyNot.0: Governance and regulation are part of the organisational context.
whyNot.1: Team skills and experience are part of the organisational context.
whyNot.3: Stakeholder availability is an organisational context factor.

B.q: Why should the chosen life cycle and its adaptations be recorded in the project management plan?
options: So the sponsor needn't attend gates
So change control can be removed
So all work to one agreed approach
So the approach can never change
B.why: Recording it in the PMP gives one agreed, approved approach that everyone understands and works to.

whyNot.0: The sponsor still takes decisions at gates.
whyNot.1: Change control is still needed whatever life cycle is chosen.
whyNot.3: The approach should be revisited if circumstances change.

C.q: A construction firm must build a school to a fixed, approved design, but the client wants teachers to shape the classroom technology. The firm has little agile experience. What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Fully iterative, as teachers want input
Fully linear, with no teacher input
C.why: The building suits linear; the technology benefits from teacher feedback. Keeping linear overall suits the firm's experience, with iteration where it adds value.

whyNot.1: Iterating a fixed, approved building design risks costly rework, and the firm lacks agile experience.
whyNot.2: Ignoring teachers loses the feedback the client has asked for.
whyNot.3: Preference is not a valid basis; the factors should drive the choice.

C.q:
A software firm with years of agile experience and an engaged product owner urgently needs early market feedback on a new product. Which THREE factors here favour iterative?
1) Engaged product owner
2) Urgent need for early feedback
3) Team's agile experience
4) A fixed-price contract with a detailed specification
C.why: An engaged product owner, urgency for early feedback and agile experience all point to iterative.

whyNot.1: Statement 4 points to linear: a fixed price against a detailed specification.
whyNot.2: Statement 4 points to linear, and the urgency (2) is missing.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 points to linear, and the engaged product owner (1) is missing.

C.q: Brightline Bank has a strong command-and-control culture and has never run an agile project, but its new app's requirements are genuinely uncertain. What should the project manager do?
options: Run fully agile and ignore culture
Adapt the model and build skills
C.why: The project needs iterative feedback, but the culture can't support pure agile yet. Adapting the model (for example adding gates) and building capability addresses both.

whyNot.0: Pure linear ignores the genuine uncertainty in the requirements.
whyNot.1: Ignoring the culture risks stalled decisions and failed time boxes.
whyNot.2: Delaying the project until culture changes is rarely realistic or necessary.

reteach.title: Choosing how to plan a holiday
reteach.question: Two families are planning holidays. One books flights, hotels and tours a year ahead. The other books flights only and decides each day what to do. Who is right?

blocks.h: It depends on who you are and what the trip needs
blocks.body: A family with young children, school dates and a tight budget (their context) visiting a busy city in peak season (the trip's needs) is wise to book everything early: that's linear. A couple who love surprises (their culture), travelling off-season where rooms are easy to find (the trip's needs), can decide day by day: that's iterative. Many families adapt: book the flights and first night, then stay flexible.

blocks.text: Neither family is wrong. The right life cycle depends on the organisation (the family) and the project (the trip), and most choices are adapted rather than pure.

explain.body: This covers the organisation around the project: its governance and regulation, contracts and procurement rules, maturity and existing methods, the skills and experience of its people, stakeholder availability and its appetite for change.

explain.caption: A memory aid for context factors, not an official APM list.

test.q: Which of these is an organisational context factor in choosing a life cycle?
options: The overall size of the project
test.why: Contract and procurement rules belong to the organisation's context.

whyNot.0: Size is a need of the project itself.
whyNot.3: Requirement certainty is a project need.

explain.body: These are features of the job itself: how certain the requirements are, how complex and risky it is, how urgently benefits are needed and how big it is. Uncertainty and urgency favour iterative; stability and costly late change favour linear.

test.q: A charity needs a donation website live before a campaign in eight weeks, and expects to refine it as donors use it. Which project needs favour iterative?
test.why: A tight deadline for early value and requirements that will evolve with donor use both favour iterative.

whyNot.0: Low complexity and small size don't by themselves point to iterative.
whyNot.1: These are organisational context factors, and they tend to favour linear.
whyNot.2: Culture is organisational context, and a control culture tends to favour linear.

explain.body: Few projects use a model exactly as drawn. Typical adaptations: add gates to iterative for a regulated client, add prototyping to linear Definition, split Deployment into releases, lighten phases on a small project, or extend the life cycle for benefits.

test.q: A linear project has a few requirements that users find hard to describe. Which adaptation would help most?
options: Fix them now and move straight on
test.why: Prototyping in Definition lets users see and react to options early, before the baseline is fixed.

whyNot.0: Removing a gate reduces control without resolving the uncertainty.
whyNot.2: Fixing unclear requirements risks building the wrong thing.
whyNot.3: Transition is handover; discovering needs then means costly rework.

explain.body: The chosen approach and its adaptations are agreed with the sponsor and recorded in the project management plan, so everyone works the same way. It is revisited at gates and reviews if the context or the project changes.

test.q: When should the suitability of the chosen life cycle be revisited?
options: Never, once the PMP is signed
At gates or when things change
Only if the sponsor is replaced
test.why: Gates and reviews are natural points to check the approach still fits, especially if the context or project needs have changed.

whyNot.0: A signed PMP can still be updated through proper control.
whyNot.1: After closure it is too late to change the approach for this project.
whyNot.3: A new sponsor is one possible trigger, but not the only one.
